items.what: Stocks that beat estimates keep drifting up for weeks to months (post-earnings-announcement drift).
items.note: Much smaller in large caps than in the 1980s. GAAP-only surprises are capped.
items.source: Yahoo earnings history (free, refreshed when a company reports)

items.what: Upward revisions to consensus EPS predict outperformance over the next 3 to 6 months.
items.note: Needs a daily history, which we are now building ourselves.

items.what: The market's reaction in the days around a report carries information about the news and persists.
Companies whose growth is speeding up tend to be rewarded; estimates lag the trend.
items.paper: Related to earnings momentum literature (Jegadeesh & Livnat 2006)
items.note: Growth is widely known, so much is priced.
items.model: In model: growth, acceleration, sales, guidance, 22 pts

items.metric: Price momentum (12 months, skipping the latest)
items.what: Winners over the past year keep outperforming losers over the next few months.
items.note: Suffers sharp crashes when markets rebound.

items.what: Stocks near their 52-week high keep outperforming; investors under-react to good news.
Fund managers' largest, most active positions beat the rest of their portfolios; changes in holdings carry information.
items.paper: Cohen, Polk & Silli 2010; Chen, Jegadeesh & Wermers 2000
items.note: Holdings are public only with a lag; the backtest here is inconclusive so far.
items.model: In model: breadth, active weight, flow, 40 pts

items.what: Clusters of insiders buying with their own money precede outperformance; sales are mostly uninformative.
items.note: Rare for large caps. Each name is checked about every 5 days.

items.what: Highly profitable, cash-generative firms outperform, partly because the market undervalues them.
items.note: Slow-moving; works better as a filter than a timing signal.

items.what: Firms issuing shares underperform; firms retiring shares outperform.
items.note: Dilution is why Intel is flagged.

items.what: Heavily shorted stocks underperform on average; shorts are often right.
items.paper: Dechow et al. 2001; Rapach et al. 2016
items.source: Yahoo short-interest data (exchange reports twice a month)

items.what: Low-risk stocks earn more than their risk implies.
items.note: Conflicts with an AI-heavy, high-beta board, so the weight is small.

items.what: Industries that did well keep doing well for months.
items.note: Also what makes the board one correlated bet.

items.what: Cheap stocks outperform over long horizons.
items.note: Poor for a decade; kept at a low weight on purpose.

items.what: Target increases predict small positive drift.
Fast balance-sheet growth and low-quality earnings precede underperformance.
items.note: Faded after publication, so the weight is small.
items.model: In model: accruals + asset growth, 3 pts

decay: McLean & Pontiff (2016) studied 97 published return predictors: returns were about 26% lower out of sample and about 58% lower after publication. Treat every effect as smaller than the papers suggest.
